explanations.answer: All the words of this law
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Moses says, “Write on them all the words of this law when you have crossed over to enter the land…” (Deuteronomy 27:3). Not a few favorites, not a highlights reel. ALL the words of this law, on big plastered stones.

explanations.answer: The names of the twelve tribes
explanations.explanation: Good guess, friend, because the tribes do come up later in this passage. But that's for where they stand on the mountains. The plastered stones are for the law, and Moses says to write on them “…all the words of this law…” The tribes get their moment a little further down.

explanations.answer: The story of the river crossing
explanations.explanation: The crossing is the timing, friend, not the writing. Moses says to set up the stones on the day they cross the Jordan, and then to write on them “…all the words of this law…” Nothing here says to write out the crossing itself. I think the river just gets to be the starting line.

I see why you'd think so, since shaping stone sounds like the normal move. But Moses says the opposite: “You must not use any iron tool on them.” The altar is to be built with uncut stones. So the chisels stay in the toolbox, friend.

You've got it, baker. Moses says, “You must not use any iron tool on them.” (Deuteronomy 27:5). Then he repeats it: the altar of the LORD goes up with uncut stones (Deuteronomy 27:6). So no iron tools on those stones. They go up just as they are.

Yes! Moses says they're to sacrifice peace offerings, “…eating them and rejoicing in the presence of the LORD your God.” So this altar isn't only burnt offerings. There's eating and there's rejoicing, right there in front of the LORD. I'd show up early for that one.

Tears do belong somewhere in life, friend, but not in this verse. Moses tells them to eat the peace offerings and rejoice in the presence of the LORD. The word he picks is rejoicing, plain and simple. So the tissues can stay home on this one.

Not this time, baker. The text doesn't tell them to tremble here. It says they're to eat the peace offerings and be “…rejoicing in the presence of the LORD your God.” I think that's a pretty happy picture.

That's the one, baker. Moses and the Levitical priests say, “Be silent, O Israel, and listen!” Before anything else gets said, the whole crowd has to get quiet. Some of us need that instruction at a family dinner, too.
Singing is a fine thing, friend, but it's not what they say here. The first instruction is “Be silent, O Israel, and listen!” It's a hush before anything else, not a song.

Good guess, baker, because the altar does come up earlier, back in verses 5 to 7. But when Moses and the Levitical priests speak to all Israel, the first thing they say is, “Be silent, O Israel, and listen!” (Deuteronomy 27:9). The altar instructions were already given before that. Here the command is to hush up and hear.
Yes, baker. Moses and the priests say, “This day you have become the people of the LORD your God.” That's a big announcement to make out loud. They are His people, and they're told so right there.
Close to sounding official, friend, but no. The line is “This day you have become the people of the LORD your God.” They're not told they're judges. They're told whose people they are.

Guests come and go, baker, and that's not the word here. Moses and the priests say, “This day you have become the people of the LORD your God.” People, not guests. It's a much bigger thing than a visit.

Right, baker. Right after calling them the LORD's people, Moses and the priests say, “You shall therefore obey the voice of the LORD your God and follow His commandments and statutes I am giving you today.” That little word “therefore” connects the two. They are His people, so they listen to His voice.

Look at that “therefore,” friend. Moses and the priests say, “You shall therefore obey the voice of the LORD your God and follow His commandments and statutes I am giving you today.” So the text itself ties obeying to being His people. It's a True one.

That's right, baker. Moses says these tribes are to stand on Mount Gerizim “…to bless the people…” (Deuteronomy 27:12). He names six: Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Joseph and Benjamin. Not a bad assignment to get.
The stones are important, friend, but nobody's given guard duty here. The tribes on Gerizim are there “…to bless the people…” That's their whole assignment in this verse.

The altar does come up in this passage, baker, but that was on Mount Ebal and earlier in Moses' speech. For the six tribes on Gerizim, the job is “…to bless the people…” No construction crew on this mountain.

Yes, baker. Moses says, “And these tribes shall stand on Mount Ebal to deliver the curse…” Reuben, Gad, Asher, Zebulun, Dan and Naphtali are the six. Gerizim handles the blessing and Ebal handles the curse.

Careful, friend, this one flips the mountains in your head easily. Moses says the six tribes on Mount Ebal stand there “…to deliver the curse…” The blessing goes with the tribes on Mount Gerizim. So the statement is True.
That's it, baker. After each curse, the text says, “And let all the people say, ‘Amen!’” The Levites speak and then everybody answers. That's the whole crowd agreeing out loud.
It's a great word, friend, and a happy one. But it's not the one in the text here. After the curse on the secret idol, the people are told to say, “Amen!”
That's a word for a different moment, baker. In this passage, the instruction after the curse is, “And let all the people say, ‘Amen!’” It's a short answer, and the whole crowd gives it together.
You got it, baker. The curse says, “Cursed is he who dishonors his father or mother.” It's about how a man treats them. And the people are to answer, “Amen!”

Nothing in this curse mentions marriage or leaving, friend. It says, “Cursed is he who dishonors his father or mother.” The thing in question is dishonoring them. Where a man lives isn't the point of the verse.
Pack the boxes if you want, baker, because this curse isn't about moving. It says, “Cursed is he who dishonors his father or mother.” The problem named is dishonor, not an address change.

That's the word, baker. The curse says, “Cursed is he who moves his neighbor’s boundary stone.” (Deuteronomy 27:17). A boundary stone marks where a neighbor's land is. Moving it is the thing that gets named. And all the people say, “Amen!”

Fixing things sounds like a friendly act, so I see the pull, friend. But the curse says, “Cursed is he who moves his neighbor’s boundary stone.” (Deuteronomy 27:17). The word in the verse is moves, not repairs.
Guarding a boundary stone sounds like a good job, baker, so no curse there. The text says, “Cursed is he who moves his neighbor’s boundary stone.” It's the moving that gets named.

explanations.answer: Lets him wander in the road
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker! Look at the verb in that curse. It isn't about pushing him or tripping him. The curse lands on the man who “…lets a blind man wander in the road.” (Deuteronomy 27:18). So letting it happen is what gets named. It's like seeing a friend about to send a message to the wrong group chat and just letting it go through.
A staff isn't mentioned anywhere in this curse, friend. The text says, “Cursed is he who lets a blind man wander in the road.” So the thing named is letting him wander.
No gate and no mocking in this verse, baker. The curse says, “Cursed is he who lets a blind man wander in the road.” The road is where it all happens.

Yes, baker. Justice is the word, and the verb matters just as much: “withholds.” The curse is on the one who holds justice back from the foreigner, the fatherless or the widow (Deuteronomy 27:19). Nothing here says he took anything. He kept it from them. And Moses says that after each curse in this list, all the people are to say, “Amen!”

Friendship is a lovely thing, friend, but it's not what the curse names. It says, “Cursed is he who withholds justice from the foreigner, the fatherless, or the widow.” The word in the verse is justice.
Handing out advice is free, baker, and I've got plenty of it. But the text says, “Cursed is he who withholds justice from the foreigner, the fatherless, or the widow.” It's justice that gets named.

Not quite, baker. The last curse says, “Cursed is he who does not put the words of this law into practice.” It doesn't name priests at all. The words are for anyone who hears them, and all the people say, “Amen!”
You've got it, friend. The final curse says, “Cursed is he who does not put the words of this law into practice.” It doesn't single out the priests. And all the people answer, “Amen!”
